title: Mini-Sermons - DSJR Student Motivation Guide
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This is Stuart's flagship explainer for "Mini-Sermons from an Apologist Winsome and Sure," the fourth of ten strategies in The Will to Learn for cultivating student motivation. He defines a mini-sermon as a brief, 30-to-60-second case a teacher makes for the value of the day's work, delivered as an "apologist" -- someone who argues for something contested -- in a manner that is winsome (joyful) and sure (confident). He presents the Rainbow of Why as the central thinking tool for generating varied mini-sermon content, so teachers don't lean on just one or two value angles repeatedly. The bulk of the article is a practical FAQ: how to get started (brainstorm, practice privately, deliver, repeat 100 times), how often to do them, what to say when a student asks whether they'll ever "use" the material, and whether it's ever too late to start -- his answer being that today is always the best available day. Throughout, Stuart insists the biggest risk isn't giving too few mini-sermons but forgetting the "mini" and turning them into extended rants that lose their power.
points: A mini-sermon is deliberately brief -- 30 to 60 seconds -- because Stuart's experience is that "frequenter, briefer mini-speeches" beat "periodic extensive ones" for building the Value belief.
The Rainbow of Why is presented as the essential brainstorming tool, since without it teachers default to just one or two value angles again and again, weakening the strategy's long-term effect.

His four-step onboarding process -- brainstorm, practice in private, deliver to students, repeat roughly 100 times -- treats mini-sermon delivery as a learnable, practiceable skill rather than an innate gift.

When a student asks "when will I ever use this," Stuart's recommended answer is sometimes an honest "maybe never," paired with confidence that the learning is still worthwhile, because Value has many colors beyond utility and relevance.
The best time to start flooding students with mini-sermons was the day they began school; the second-best time, and the only one any teacher can control, is today.
quotes: A mini-sermon is a brief (30- to 60-second) speech in which the teacher "makes the case" for the Value of the course, the work, the learning.
Please don't miss the mini! Many teachers (myself included) are guilty of going on inspired but extended rants about the goodness of their subjects. These are too long and too time-consuming.
Winsome, from the Old English word wyn, meaning "joy." We want our language to emanate joy. Speaking like this is a learnable skill and a cultivatable disposition.
If you crash and burn during a mini-sermon, good news: it's only 30 or so seconds lost. And when you crash and burn, make note of what went wrong. Learning what doesn't work = progress.

Look at the Rainbow of Why. There are so many more pathways to Value than utility and relevance. To drive this home, I love periodically reminding my students that they will likely never "use" what we're learning in some of our lessons.

The more of these kinds of signals you receive as a human being, the more likely you are to interpret them as the norm. If you're flooded with this stuff consistently from the time you're young, you're super likely to both experience and embody a culture in which learning is deeply and beautifully and meaningfully good.

Mini-sermons are a win-win: they help us (our own teaching skills, our own teacher motivation) and that help students. Just don't forget the MINI part of mini-sermons: these things are meant to be short (30-90 seconds).
